requested.title: cookies.delete() drops secure/partitioned from the resolved defaults, so __Host-/__Secure-/Partitioned cookies are never actually cleared
hostHeader without protocolHeader produces a scheme-mismatched CSRF origin, 403ing every production form POST while silencing the boot warning built to catch exactly that
An xffDepth larger than the real proxy chain lets a padded X-Forwarded-For set getClientAddress() to any attacker-chosen value
getClientAddress() returns the forwarded header verbatim with no IP-format or length validation, and the value is used directly as a rate-limit store key
A configured hostHeader that the proxy does not send silently degrades to the client-controlled Host header while CSRF reports the origin as trusted
WebSocket upgrades are entirely exempt from the Origin check (CSWSH)
`proxy.hostHeader` alone silently 403s every production form POST, and suppresses the boot warning designed to catch exactly that
The protection gate short-circuits before the rate limiter, so unverified clients are never metered and never accumulate ban violations
reportEarlyExit's kind filter rests on a stale invariant — protection-gate blocks on ws/sse/island emit no request event
Enhanced form submissions navigate via `window.location.assign()` with no scheme validation, upgrading an open redirect into same-origin XSS

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified end-to-end. `delete()` (cookies.ts:107-113) builds the serialize options as `{ path: defaults.path, domain: defaults.domain, ...options, maxAge: 0 }`, so `secure`, `partitioned`, `sameSite`, `httpOnly` and `priority` from the resolved `cookieDefaults` are all dropped. `serializeCookie` only sets `init.secure = options.secure`, and Bun's own types/docs confirm the defaults: `node_modules/bun-types/bun.d.ts:10745-10758` documents `path` defaulting to `/` and `sameSite` to `lax`, and `new Bun.Cookie('name','value').toString()` is documented as `"name=value; Path=/; SameSite=Lax"` — i.e. no `Secure`, no `Partitioned`. The repo's own test suite proves the attribute is omitted when the flag is falsy (cookies.test.ts: `jar.set('session','abc',{secure:false})` → `not.toContain('Secure')`), so the deletion header is `__Host-session=; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=0`. RFC 6265bis's cookie-prefix rules require a UA to ignore a `Set-Cookie` for a `__Secure-`/`__Host-` name whose secure-only-flag is false, so that header is discarded and the session cookie survives — while L104's `this.parsed.delete(name)` makes the server (and the debug bar) believe it is gone. The API offers no escape hatch: `delete`'s options are typed `Pick<CookieSerializeOptions,'path'|'domain'>`, so a caller cannot pass `secure: true` through it and must fall back to `set(name,'',{maxAge:0,secure:true})`. The CHIPS half is also correct — an unpartitioned `Set-Cookie` does not evict a cookie stored under a partition key, and is itself rejected outright in a third-party context when 3P cookies are blocked. Confirmed as a framework-API defect; blast radius is limited to consumers using prefixed or partitioned cookies (I grepped: no `__Host-`/`__Secure-`/`partitioned` usage anywhere in this monorepo, so no in-repo app is currently broken), and the only existing `delete()` test asserts path/domain only. MEDIUM is appropriate: failed logout/session-invalidation for apps that follow the recommended prefix hardening.

Every link in the chain checks out. `resolveExpectedOrigin` returns early on `options.origin` (proxy.ts:58) but otherwise takes the protocol from `url.protocol` whenever `protocolHeader` is unset (L74), and `url` comes from `new URL(request.url)` — plain `http:` for a Bun server behind a TLS-terminating proxy. `normalizeOrigin` (csrf.ts:37-45) strips only `:443`/`:80` and never reconciles schemes, so csrf.ts:153 compares `http://app.example` against the browser-sent `https://app.example` and always fails, yielding the 403 at csrf.ts:171 for every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE with a form content type. The silencing half is equally real: `csrfBootWarning` returns null the moment `proxy.hostHeader` is set (csrf.ts:81) and `expectedOriginConfigured` is `Boolean(proxy?.origin || proxy?.hostHeader)` (csrf.ts:133), so neither the boot warning nor the prod-hard-block path fires. Dev is clean too — I traced it: in dev no `x-forwarded-host` arrives, `rawHost` falls back to `url.host` (`localhost:3333`), expected origin equals the browser's Origin, and the request passes with no warning at all, so nothing surfaces before deploy. The behaviour is pinned by proxy.test.ts ('hostHeader alone uses url.protocol' → `http://public.example`), and the docs actively advertise the broken config: 160-serve-options.md:182 and 152-protection.md:97 both say `proxy.origin` *or* `proxy.hostHeader` satisfies the CSRF requirement. I confirmed the finding's scoping claim — site, support and demos all pass `proxy.origin` explicitly (site/index.ts:201, support/index.ts:38, demos/index.ts:27), so the impact lands on external `mochi-framework` consumers, not this repo. Fails closed, so it is an availability/correctness bug rather than an exposure; HIGH_BUG is defensible given it silently breaks every form mutation in production.

The arithmetic is exactly as described. `ips[ips.length - depth] ?? ips[ips.length - 1]` (proxy.ts:106) only falls through to the `??` branch when the computed index is negative, i.e. strictly when `depth > ips.length`; at `depth === ips.length` the index is 0 — the leftmost, wholly client-supplied entry. Since the attacker controls the chain length by pre-seeding the header, one padding entry converts the 'safe' over-configured case into full control: with one appending proxy (nginx's `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` preserves the inbound value and appends `$remote_addr`) and `xffDepth: 2`, a request carrying `X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.9` arrives as `198.51.100.9, <realClient>`, length 2, depth 2, index 0 → the attacker's own string is returned. So the in-code safety claim at L104-105 and the test that pins it (proxy.test.ts 'xffDepth deeper than the chain … never the spoofable leftmost') are both wrong for the padded case. The downstream impact is confirmed: `createRouteLimiter`'s default key generator reads the stashed `getClientAddress()` value (rateLimit.ts:218-222, 249-251), and hitlimit bans by that same key, so rotating the header evades limits and sending a victim's IP burns the victim's quota and can trip the configured `ban` (rateLimit.ts:234) against them. Preconditions are honest in the finding and I verified them: a correctly-matched depth is robust, and this repo's apps all use `xffDepth: 1`. The precondition is an operator error that 160-serve-options.md does warn about in prose ('Pass the right xffDepth'), which caps the practical severity — but the defect is that the framework's documented *mitigation* for getting it wrong does not actually hold, so MEDIUM stands.

The mechanism is confirmed, with narrower preconditions than the write-up implies. `getClientAddress` returns the split XFF entry (L106) or the raw header (L109) with no IP-shape or length validation, and that string becomes the hitlimit key verbatim (rateLimit.ts:250 → :222), which for the sqlite/postgres stores is a persisted row key. I verified the namespace format in the pinned dependency rather than assuming it: `node_modules/@joint-ops/hitlimit-bun/dist/index.js:179` does `key = \`group:${groupId}:${key}\``, and it is applied only when `config.group` is truthy — which for Mochi means a route's own `rateLimit` gets `group = <route pattern>` (its `autoGroup`) while the shared global limiter passes nothing (Mochi.ts:808 vs :823, rateLimit.ts:213). So an address string of `group:/some/route:<victimIP>` sent to a globally-limited route collides exactly with the row the grouped route uses for that victim, defeating an invariant the docs state as a guarantee (122-rate-limiting.md:85: 'different routes backed by the same database keep separate counters'). Two preconditions gate it: the attacker must be able to influence the address at all — which itself requires a misconfiguration the module docstring and a `danger` callout warn against, or the F3 padding trick — and the two limiters must share one store instance (plausible: 122-rate-limiting.md:93-98 explicitly tells you to create one store and share it). Given that precondition the attacker already owns the rate-limit identity, so the incremental impact (cross-route poisoning, multi-KB persisted keys) is modest, and one supporting detail is wrong: support/routes.ts:110 *renders* `getClientAddress()` on the admin page, it does not persist it. Still a real, cheaply-fixable defect — validating the extracted value as an IPv4/IPv6 literal closes the forgery and the unbounded-key growth outright.

The code description is accurate — an absent configured `hostHeader` falls back to `url.host` (proxy.ts:75), which Bun derives from the inbound `Host` header, while csrf.ts:133 has already decided `expectedOriginConfigured` from the mere presence of the option — but there is no attack behind it. CSRF defends against one adversary: a victim's browser. Browsers pin `Host` to the real target and treat it as a forbidden header, so the only requests that can exercise the degraded comparison are ones the attacker crafts directly — and for those the check is a no-op *even in a perfectly configured deployment*, because any client that can set `Host` can equally set `Origin` to the configured value. The finding concedes this itself, which leaves only the secondary claims, and those don't survive either. Deriving `url.origin` from the client's `Host` is the framework's pre-existing default whenever no proxy options are set, so this is not a degradation this code path introduces; it is the app's job not to emit `event.url.origin` into trusted output, and the one in-repo place that would matter — the newsletter double-opt-in and unsubscribe links — builds URLs from `MOCHI_ORIGIN` via `newsletter/config.ts:8-17`, not from the request. Nor is the configuration reliably attacker-facing: a proxy that doesn't send `X-Forwarded-Host` usually also rewrites `Host` to the upstream name (nginx's default `$proxy_host`), in which case the expected origin becomes the internal address and the check fails closed, not open. The `portHeader` sub-claim is real but harmless: `new URL('/p', 'http://h:abc')` does throw inside the unwrapped `buildRequestContext` (e.g. Mochi.ts:1439-1443), yet the only request it 500s is the attacker's own — no victim, no state change. Finally, every deployed app here sets `proxy.origin`, which short-circuits header derivation entirely. The hardening suggestions (warn on a configured-but-absent header, validate host/port shape, wrap the `new URL`) are worth doing, so I've re-labelled it as a non-security robustness item rather than a vulnerability.

Both independent reasons check out. `KIND_POLICY` sets `ws: { csrf: false }` (requestSetup.ts:66), so `csrfCheck` is never invoked for a handshake, and `DEFAULT_PROTECTED_METHODS` (csrf.ts:26) covers only POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE while a handshake is a GET — so even flipping the policy flag would not help. I traced the whole upgrade path (Mochi.ts:1262-1328): `buildRequestContext` with `kind: 'ws'`, `route:matched`, the app's optional `upgrade(req, wsParams)`, then `server.upgrade()` — the `Origin` header is never read, and a repo-wide grep for `origin` in Mochi.ts returns only the three CSRF call sites. The documentation gap is worse than stated: 100-websocket-routes.md has zero occurrences of 'origin', and it actively steers authors toward exactly the vulnerable pattern — 'Reject unauthenticated sockets in `upgrade`' (L71-75) plus '`getRequestContext()` works inside `upgrade`, so cookies … are available there' (L81). Browsers apply neither SOP nor CORS to WebSockets, so `new WebSocket('wss://target/ws/chat')` from an attacker page connects and is readable/writable. One mitigation the finding misses and that should temper the severity: because `serializeCookie` leaves `init.sameSite` unset unless the caller specifies it, Bun emits an explicit `SameSite=Lax` on every jar-set cookie, and every current browser honours an explicit Lax attribute by suppressing the cookie on a cross-site, non-top-level-navigation request — including a WS handshake. Real-world exploitability therefore needs a cookie set with `sameSite: 'none'` (plausible here: this monorepo's own newsletter widget is a cross-origin iframe), a cookie set outside the jar with no SameSite, or other ambient credentials such as cached HTTP Basic. The gap is genuine and the recommended `csrf.checkWebSocketOrigin` default-on fix is the right shape; MEDIUM is fair.

This is the same underlying defect as F2, seen from csrf.ts rather than proxy.ts — and because the duplicate verdict is only valid within a single file, both get real verdicts. The csrf.ts-side facts are all confirmed: `csrfBootWarning` short-circuits to null on `options.proxy?.hostHeader` (L81), `expectedOriginConfigured` is `Boolean(proxy?.origin || proxy?.hostHeader)` (L133), `normalizeOrigin` (L37-45) touches only the default-port suffix so a scheme mismatch can never be reconciled at L153, and the dev branch at L160-165 merely warns. Combined with `resolveExpectedOrigin`'s protocol fallback to `url.protocol` (proxy.ts:74), a `hostHeader`-only deployment behind TLS termination compares `http://app.example` to `https://app.example` and 403s every protected form submission — the precise production-only breakage the L70-73 doc comment says the boot warning exists to surface, suppressed by the very configuration that causes it. Worth adding: the same partial config also silently breaks protection mode, since 152-protection.md:97 notes the verify POST rides the same CSRF check, so an uncleared visitor would exhaust `maxAttempts` and be told their browser can't be verified. The recommendation is sound and the cheapest variant is the scheme-agnostic comparison when no `protocolHeader` was configured, or requiring `protocolHeader`/`origin` before treating the origin as configured. Leaving the filed BUG severity alone — F2 carries the headline severity for this defect.

The ordering claim is exactly right. `buildRequestContext` runs the protection gate at requestSetup.ts:130-136 and returns `{ earlyResponse }`, and both route handlers check `'earlyResponse' in setup` and return before anything else (Mochi.ts:971-973 for pages, :1202-1204 for api) — `checkRouteLimit` is only reached afterwards, at :981 and :1211 respectively. So a client without clearance is answered without `limiter.check()` ever running, which means hitlimit's counter and its violation/ban bookkeeping (rateLimit.ts:234, and `ban`/`recordViolation` in the store interface) never advance for exactly the traffic an operator configured them to stop: the two controls silently cancel. The cost side is confirmed too — gate.ts:129 routes every GET/HEAD page or fallback hit to `interstitialResponse`, which does a `mintCaptcha()` (AES-SIV seal + randomUUID, captcha.ts:43-52) plus a full `registry.renderComponent()` and `renderShell()` per request, against a limiter check that would have been a single store increment. I also verified the companion path the finding checked: the verify endpoint is registered straight into `bunRoutes` (Mochi.ts:1812-1813), so it isn't in `routeLimiters` and is unmetered as well, but `verifyCaptcha` is one decrypt plus a short hash check, so the amplification really does live in the interstitial render. 152-protection.md documents the gate as covering every route kind and positions it as a Cloudflare-style bot defence, with nothing said about metering, so this is a design gap rather than a stated trade-off. Requests are still 403'd, so nothing protected is reached — the impact is unmetered CPU plus an inert ban control, which keeps it at MEDIUM rather than higher.

Confirmed, including the staleness. `reportEarlyExit` bails for any kind other than page/api/file (requestSetup.ts:94-96) on the stated grounds that 'only page and api can early-exit at all (trailingSlash, csrf)' — the comment doesn't even match its own code, which also admits `file`. That invariant is now false: the protection gate at L130-136 is guarded only by `cfg.protection && !opts.skipProtection`, with no `KIND_POLICY` entry, and `KIND_POLICY` gives `ws`, `sse`, `island` and `file` both `trailingSlash: false` and `csrf: false`, so the gate is the *only* early-exit route for those kinds. 152-protection.md confirms the gate is meant to fire for all of them ('pages, APIs, WebSockets, SSE, and unmatched URLs'), and `MochiRequestKind` in events.ts:5 is indeed `page|api|file|asset|image|fallback|error`, excluding ws/sse/island. Two refinements from tracing the emitters: successful island requests never emit a `request` event either (Mochi.ts:1689-1694 just returns), so for islands this is a hole in an uninstrumented surface rather than a one-sided blind spot; but ws and sse already report their own rejections through the existing `kind: 'error'` escape hatch (`emitWsReject` at Mochi.ts:1271-1280, the SSE HEAD 405 at :1346-1354), so the precedent for emitting these exists and the only reason protection blocks go unreported is the stale narrowing. Net effect is as described — in protection mode, blocked island/ws/sse traffic is invisible to `consoleLogger()` and to any event-bus observability, which is the signal an operator would use to distinguish a misconfigured `protect()` from an attack. BUG severity is right.

The sink and the absence of validation are verified at every hop. `redirect(status, location)` stores the argument verbatim (forms.ts:21-23), the action path hands it to `jsonRedirect` for enhanced submissions (Mochi.ts:1132-1136), `jsonRedirect` serialises it unchecked (formsJson.ts:56-58), `deserialize` only devalue-decodes `data` (enhance.client.ts:9-15), and the default fallback passes it straight to `window.location.assign(result.location)` (L60-62) with no scheme test — `location.assign` is a standard DOM-XSS sink and a `javascript:` URL navigation initiated by same-origin script evaluates in the current document (blocked only by a CSP without `unsafe-inline`, and the framework sets no default CSP). The asymmetry the finding rests on is also correct: on the native path the same value becomes a `Location` header (Mochi.ts:1137-1140), and per Fetch's HTTP-redirect-fetch a non-HTTP(S) `Location` scheme is a network error, so `javascript:` is inert there. 74-use-enhance.md:49-56 documents `window.location.assign(result.location)` as the contract with no caveat about validating the target, which is what leaves app authors unaware that adding `{@attach enhance()}` upgrades an open redirect into same-origin script execution. The honest caveat is that reaching it requires app code that forwards untrusted input into `redirect()` — I grepped every `redirect(` call site in this monorepo and all of them use literals or safely-encoded internal paths (the closest is `demos/data-loading/routes.ts:15`, which `encodeURIComponent`s into a path), so nothing here is exploitable today. It remains a real framework-level hardening defect: the fix (reject anything whose `protocol` isn't `http:`/`https:` after `new URL(location, window.location.href)`, and validate server-side in `redirect()` so both paths agree) matches what SvelteKit's `goto`-based `applyAction` already enforces. MEDIUM, contingent on app misuse.
